newsitem.title: CHINA: China ducks queries on Red Cross jail inspections.
newsitem.headline: China ducks queries on Red Cross jail inspections.

text.p: China said on Tuesday it was willing to expand contacts with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) but ducked questions on whether it would restart talks on unfettered visits to political prisoners.
The New York Times said this week China had agreed to reopen long-stalled negotiations with the ICRC over access to prisoners convicted of offences related to politics or religion.

Permitting ICRC visits would fulfill one condition for a possible Sino-U.S. deal on human rights under which Washington would agree not to sponsor a U.N. resolution condemning Beijing's rights record, the newspaper said.
A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to comment on reports Beijing was reconsidering its stance on ICRC visits.
"China and the International Committee of the Red Cross have always maintained relations of friendly cooperation," spokesman Tang Guoqiang told a news briefing in the Chinese capital.
"Both sides hope to expand mutual exchanges and cooperation," he said but gave no further details.

Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen raised international hopes for new openness in China's policies towards prisoners in 1993 when he said Beijing had agreed in principle to inspections by the ICRC, which demands unfettered and unaccompanied access to prisoners.

Talks on such inspections later stalled, with senior justice officials saying China was not obliged to give access because none of the thousands of "counter-revolutionaries" in its jails was a political prisoner as defined by the United Nations.

Western human rights activists have long accused China of tolerating widespread and serious abuse of prisoners convicted for political offences, particularly those detained in the restive far-western regions of Tibet and Xinjiang.
China last year tightened its curbs on political dissent, jailing, detaining or forcing into exile almost all remaining members of its tiny and struggling pro-democracy movement.

The New York Times said late last month that Beijing and Washington were close to a deal aimed at easing friction over human rights -- long a major irritant to the sensitive cross-Pacific relationship.

Under the possible deal the United States would drop moves to censure Beijing at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva this spring in exchange for Chinese concessions including ICRC prison visits and the signing of two human rights covenants.
China has said it is actively considering signing the covenents but needs more time to research their implications.
